nodes.name: Oxygen defect introduction by H2O2 etching
nodes.procedure: Oxygen defects were first introduced into NiFe-LDH grown on nickel foam through controlled H₂O₂ etching using 0, 80, 120, 160, and 200 μL H₂O₂. The optimal D-NiFe-LDH was prepared using 160 μL H₂O₂.
nodes.source_text: by first introducing oxygen defects into NiFe-LDH through controlled H₂O₂ etching (0, 80, 120, 160, and 200 μL)

nodes.name: Hydrothermal Pt loading
nodes.procedure: Atomically dispersed Pt atoms were anchored onto oxygen-deficient NiFe-LDH (D-NiFe-LDH) through a hydrothermal method by precise regulation of PtCl₄ solution concentration. The optimal sample designated as Pt/D-NiFe-LDH contained 1.27 wt.% Pt and was prepared using 160 μL H₂O₂ in the previous etching step. Inductively coupled plasma analysis confirms the Pt loadings.

nodes.description: HER stability testing in 1 M KOH at 100 mA/cm²
nodes.source_text: Pt/D-NiFe-LDH and Pt/C were subjected to chronopotentiometry tests at 100 mA cm^{-2}. Figure 3h,i show that the HER performance of Pt/C significantly deteriorates after only a dozen hours at 100 mA cm^{-2}. In contrast, the overpotential of Pt/D-NiFe-LDH increases only slowly after 300 h of testing

nodes.description: HER stability testing with 5000 CV cycles
nodes.source_text: To assess the stability of Pt/D-NiFe-LDH, we conducted 5000 cyclic voltammetry (CV) cycles and compared the changes in the LSV curves prior to and following the reaction. As can be seen from the insets in Figures 3h,i, the LSV curves remain almost unchanged after 5000 CV cycles

nodes.characterization_summary: Pt loadings confirmed as 0.38, 1.08, 1.27, and 3.83 wt.% for samples with varying PtCl4 concentrations.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Inductively coupled plasma analysis confirms the Pt loadings (Figure S1, Supporting Information)

nodes.characterization_summary: Isolated bright spots confirm atomic dispersion of Pt species with lattice fringes 1.53 Å and 2.66 Å matching (110) and (101) planes of D-NiFe-LDH.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As can be seen from the spherical aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (AC-HAADF-STEM) plots (Figure 1c; Figure S6, Supporting Information) of the samples, the lattice fringes 1.53Å and 2.66Å within them match the (110) and (101) crystallographic planes of D-NiFe-LDH, respectively.

nodes.characterization_summary: Uniform dispersion of Ni, Fe, O throughout the material with atomically dispersed Pt atoms across D-NiFe-LDH framework.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Figure 1d illustrates the elemental distribution within the sample, revealing uniform dispersion of Ni, Fe, and O throughout the material.

nodes.characterization_summary: Characteristic peaks of NiFe-LDH at 11.60°, 23.39°, 33.73°, 34.48°, 38.94°, 46.39°, 59.89°, and 61.17° with no Pt-related peaks confirming atomic dispersion; (110) peak shifts to higher angles and (003) to lower angles.
nodes.evidence_snippet: X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis of powdered samples reveals characteristic peaks corresponding to the (003), (006), (101), (012), (015), (018), (110), and (113) planes of NiFe-LDH (JCPDS No. 40-0215) at 11.60°, 23.39°, 33.73°, 34.48°, 38.94°, 46.39°, 59.89°, and 61.17°, respectively (Figure 1e).

nodes.evidence_snippet: Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy reveals a distinct signal at g = 2.003 (Figure 1f), characteristic of oxygen defects.

properties.type: Gibbs free energy vs reaction coordinate

nodes.characterization_summary: Peaks at 310 cm⁻¹ (e_g bending of NiO-H), 462 cm⁻¹ (tensile vibration of Ni-O a1g), and 528 cm⁻¹ (e_g bending of Ni-OH); 528 cm⁻¹ peak disappears and 462 cm⁻¹ red shifts in Pt-loaded sample.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Figure 1g presents the Raman spectra of the samples. The e_g bending of NiO-H is responsible for the peak at 310 cm⁻¹. The tensile vibration of Ni-O a1g and the e_g bending of Ni-OH are responsible for the two peaks at 462 cm⁻¹ and 528 cm⁻¹, respectively.

nodes.characterization_summary: Pt 4f XPS shows peaks at 70.60 eV (4f7/2) and 74.02 eV (4f5/2) indicating negative valence Pt with -0.80 eV shift vs Pt foil (71.40 eV); Ni 2p3/2 shifts from 856.20 eV (NiFe-LDH) to 856.36 eV (Pt/NiFe-LDH) to 857.11 eV (Pt/D-NiFe-LDH); O 1s oxygen vacancy percentage increases from 40.22% (Pt/NiFe-LDH) to 62.49% (Pt/D-NiFe-LDH).
nodes.evidence_snippet: For Pt/D-NiFe-LDH, the 4f7/2 and 4f5/2 electrons of Pt are responsible for the peaks at 70.60 and 74.02 eV, respectively. Compared with the binding energy of 71.40 eV for the 4f7/2 electron of metal Pt, the above binding energy values indicate that Pt in Pt/D-NiFe-LDH is in a negative valence state.

nodes.characterization_summary: Pt L3-edge white line peak intensity lower than Pt foil, more so for Pt/D-NiFe-LDH, indicating stronger negative valence state.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The samples' Pt L3-edge X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectra are displayed in Figure 2d.

nodes.characterization_summary: FT-EXAFS peak at 2.70 Å corresponds to Pt-Ni(Fe) scattering shell (not Pt-Pt); wavelet transform confirms Pt-Ni(Fe) as main coordination environment.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Figure 2e exhibits a distinct peak at 2.70Å, which differs from the characteristic peak position of Pt-Pt bonds.

nodes.characterization_summary: Interconnected standing nanosheet morphology with nanopores; thinner sheets and larger nanopores compared to pristine NiFe-LDH, no granular features indicating no Pt clustering.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As depicted in Figure 1b, Pt/D-NiFe-LDH has an interconnected standing nanosheet morphology, with a large number of nanopores between these nanosheets.
